title: Let the Language Model Write the Counterfactual

body:
The problem begins with a question whose phrasing betrays it. Does *politeness* in a complaint change how fast a bureaucracy responds? Does the *gender* of a candidate's biography change how voters rate them? Each question treats one feature of a text as a treatment and the rest as nuisance. The reader can imagine the experiment they would like to run — two biographies identical except for the pronoun, served to voters at random — and then imagine the paper that will never publish, because the two biographies, even if hand-written, differ in a dozen correlated things.

Causal inference with text has spent fifteen years trying to work around this. You collect the texts you have, you learn a representation that tries to isolate the feature, and you adjust for whatever's left. Pryzant et al.'s *TextCause* fits BERT as a confounding adjustment; Fong and Grimmer's supervised Indian Buffet Process searches a corpus for latent treatments. The 2024–2026 wave of LLM-based causal estimation makes a different move: stop searching the text for the treatment, and *generate* it. Imai and Nakamura's "Causal Representation Learning with Generative Artificial Intelligence" (JASA, 2026) and Veljanovski and Wood-Doughty's DoubleLingo (NAACL 2024) are the two load-bearing papers. They share a framing — put a language model inside a Chernozhukov-style double machine learning pipeline — and disagree instructively on where it goes.

## Why this matters now

Three things changed at once. Large language models can now write counterfactual versions of a prompt that differ in one controllable feature with enough fidelity that a trained reader cannot reliably tell which came from a human. The decoder-only architectures expose a hidden state large enough to act as a nuisance representation. And the econometric literature on orthogonal scores — Chernozhukov et al.'s 2018 double/debiased machine learning — has absorbed deep nuisance estimators cleanly enough that one can slot an LLM into the estimator and still write down a central-limit theorem. The combination is what makes "the LLM writes the counterfactual" a real inference procedure rather than a vignette.

It also matters because the alternative is worse than it looks. Representations learned to predict both treatment and outcome tend to absorb the treatment, and once they do, the positivity (overlap) assumption fails: units in the two treatment arms occupy disjoint regions of the representation, and the inverse propensity weights explode. Tierney, Katta, and Bail show this directly in simulations in a 2025 paper arguing for experimental designs over post-hoc adjustment. The LLM-generated route tries to walk between the two cliffs.

## The setup

Let $T \in \{0,1\}$ be a scalar treatment feature of a text $X$ (say, politeness), $Y$ the outcome (say, response time), and $Z$ pre-text covariates. The target is the average treatment effect,

$$\tau = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)].$$

The problem is that $X$ is high-dimensional and contains much more than $T$; any feature of $X$ correlated with $T$ and affecting $Y$ is a confounder. Pryzant-style methods adjust for an embedding $\phi(X)$ learned to predict $Y$. Imai and Nakamura's complaint is structural: if $\phi$ is good, it also predicts $T$, which drives the propensity $\Pr(T = 1 \mid \phi(X))$ to $0$ or $1$ on the training support. Overlap fails. The confidence interval is either absurdly wide or quietly wrong.

Their fix is to never let a single representation carry both signals. Generate the texts under treatment and control prompts with an LLM, extract the hidden state $R \in \mathbb{R}^r$ at a chosen layer, and then *separate* $R$ into two pieces with a TarNet-style architecture: a treatment representation $f_T(R)$ meant to carry $T$, and a *deconfounder* $f(R) \in \mathbb{R}^q$, $q \le r$, meant to carry everything else. The identification claim is Lemma-style:

$$Y \,\perp\!\!\!\perp\, R \;\mid\; T,\, f(R).$$

Once you condition on the deconfounder and the treatment, the rest of the hidden state no longer matters for the outcome. Adjust for $f(R)$ and $Z$, and the ATE is nonparametrically identified, under a separability assumption the authors make explicit — that the LLM's representation can be decomposed into treatment-carrying and confounder-carrying pieces. The deconfounder is not unique, and this is a feature: any valid $f$ works, which is the technical reason the estimator does not require the LLM to disentangle meaningfully, only to disentangle at all.

## The orthogonal score

The reason to care about the DML framing is that it protects against slow-converging neural nuisance estimators. Chernozhukov's construction writes the ATE as a Neyman-orthogonal moment,

$$\psi(O; \tau, \eta) \;=\; \mu_1 - \mu_0 \;+\; \frac{T\,(Y - \mu_1)}{e} \;-\; \frac{(1-T)\,(Y - \mu_0)}{1 - e} \;-\; \tau,$$

with outcome regressions $\mu_t(Z, f(R)) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = t, Z, f(R)]$ and propensity $e(Z, f(R)) = \Pr(T = 1 \mid Z, f(R))$. Neyman orthogonality means $\partial_\eta\, \mathbb{E}[\psi] = 0$ at the truth; a small error in the nuisance $\eta = (\mu_0, \mu_1, e, f)$ produces a second-order error in the moment, so if each nuisance converges at rate $n^{-1/4}$, the product-of-errors rate is $n^{-1/2}$ and the estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-asymptotically normal. Cross-fitting on $K$ folds — fit $\eta$ on $K-1$ folds, plug into $\psi$ on the held-out fold, rotate — kills the overfitting bias. The payoff is a real confidence interval you can actually believe when your nuisance models are a multi-billion-parameter language model and a two-head neural net.

## A concrete anchor

Imai and Nakamura's demonstrator is the Fong and Grimmer Congressional candidate biographies: 1,246 texts with "text reuse" from party templates flagged as a binary treatment. They estimate the ATE of text reuse on perceived favourability. Their GPI pipeline returns $\hat\tau \approx 5.46$ with a 95% interval of $[2.79, 8.13]$; a naive DML baseline, fitting outcome and propensity directly on the BERT representation of the raw $X$, returns $\hat\tau \approx -67.8$ with an enormous interval — the overlap-failure signature, sign flip included. The failure reproduces across LLM backbones in the paper's appendix.

A toy version of the outer loop in NumPy is short enough to read:

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold

def dml_ate(T, Y, Phi, K=5):
    n = len(Y); psi = np.zeros(n)
    for tr, te in KFold(K, shuffle=True).split(Phi):
        e  = LogisticRegression().fit(Phi[tr], T[tr]).predict_proba(Phi[te])[:, 1]
        e  = np.clip(e, 0.05, 0.95)                      # propensity trimming
        m1 = Ridge().fit(Phi[tr][T[tr]==1], Y[tr][T[tr]==1]).predict(Phi[te])
        m0 = Ridge().fit(Phi[tr][T[tr]==0], Y[tr][T[tr]==0]).predict(Phi[te])
        psi[te] = m1 - m0 + T[te]*(Y[te]-m1)/e - (1-T[te])*(Y[te]-m0)/(1-e)
    return psi.mean(), psi.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)
```

Feed `Phi = deconfounder(hidden_states(X))` and you have the Imai–Nakamura estimator at the level a reader can run on their laptop; feed `Phi = BERT_cls(X)` and you have the baseline that the paper beats. DoubleLingo is the same moment when $T$ is observed and $X$ is a *confounder* rather than a treatment: a single LLM is deliberately *not* reused for both $\mu_t$ and $e$, because the shared representation re-creates the overlap problem the orthogonal score is supposed to dampen. The authors report a 10% relative reduction in absolute error on the Reddit text-confounding benchmark.

What the code does not show is the first half of the pipeline, where the LLM writes the texts. For the treatment-as-feature setting, the paper prompts the model twice — once with a template that instantiates $T=1$ and once with the matched $T=0$ template — and reads off the hidden states at a fixed layer. The matched pair is the step that produces overlap by construction: every text in the treated arm has a paired text in the control arm generated from the same covariates, so the propensity in the matched sample is bounded away from 0 and 1 by design, not by assumption. The orthogonal-score layer on top is then protecting a ground that has already been firmed up.

## What it implies in practice

Three habits to reach for. First, when your treatment is a feature of a text — a linguistic property, a stylistic choice, a demographic signal — prefer *generating* the counterfactual to adjusting for the original. The counterfactual-generator move avoids the circular problem that the feature most predictive of your treatment is your treatment. Second, do not fit a single representation to predict both treatment and outcome; separate the two heads, as TarNet does, and route only the confounder head into the propensity model. Third, run the DML diagnostic even if you are not going to write an econometrics paper: inspect the propensity histogram, trim at 0.05–0.95, and compute the effective sample size after inverse-weighting. An LLM-based causal estimator fails at exactly the same point a lesser one does, and the diagnostic is cheap.

## Limits and open questions

The separability assumption is the method's load-bearing hypothesis, and it is untested in the empirical sense. Nothing in the architecture *guarantees* that the TarNet split actually isolates the treatment; the authors show calibration on held-out counterfactuals, but that is a necessary and not a sufficient check. Generated counterfactuals also inherit the LLM's biases — the "neutral" version of a politically coded sentence is whatever the model's RLHF decided neutrality should mean, which is a form of unmeasured treatment you cannot adjust for from inside the model that created it. Tierney, Katta, and Bail's point that human-produced counterfactuals remain the gold standard is not refuted by any of this. The DML normality guarantee needs the $n^{-1/4}$ rate on every nuisance, which for a frozen LLM's hidden-state representation is an assumption about the geometry of the model more than a theorem about an estimator. And the construct-validity question — whether a feature a social scientist named "politeness" is the feature the LLM edits when prompted to make a text more polite — sits outside the framework entirely; it is a measurement problem, and no amount of orthogonal moments repairs it. The most honest reading is that GPI and DoubleLingo give you a pipeline whose assumptions are checkable in principle, not a free lunch on the text-as-treatment problem.

## Further reading

- Kosuke Imai and Kentaro Nakamura, *Causal Representation Learning with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Application to Texts as Treatments*, Journal of the American Statistical Association, accepted 2026; arXiv:2410.00903. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00903>. The GPI paper. Read the identification lemma and the Fong–Grimmer reanalysis in the appendix; the slides at the authors' site summarise the TarNet architecture more compactly than the paper.
- Marko Veljanovski and Zach Wood-Doughty, *DoubleLingo: Causal Estimation with Large Language Models*, NAACL 2024 Short Papers, 799–807. <https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-short.71/>. The companion move for when text is a confounder rather than a treatment; argues against reusing a single LLM for both nuisance heads, with a 10% error reduction on the benchmark.
- Reid Pryzant, Dallas Card, Dan Jurafsky, Victor Veitch, and Dhanya Sridhar, *Causal Effects of Linguistic Properties*, NAACL 2021; arXiv:2010.12919. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12919>. The TextCause baseline. Worth reading to see what the single-representation approach does well and where the overlap problem first bites.
- Victor Chernozhukov, Denis Chetverikov, Mert Demirer, Esther Duflo, Christian Hansen, Whitney Newey, and James Robins, *Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Treatment and Structural Parameters*, The Econometrics Journal, 21(1):C1–C68, 2018; arXiv:1608.00060. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.00060>. The source of the orthogonal score and cross-fitting construction every paper above depends on.
- Graham Tierney, Pradeep Katta, and Christopher Bail, *An Experimental Design Alternative to Post-Hoc Adjustment for Text-as-Treatment*, 2025; arXiv:2510.08758. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08758>. The in-field critique: shows the overlap-violation failure in simulation and argues that human-written counterfactuals and RCTs remain the honest baseline.
- Wen Guo and collaborators, *Estimating Causal Effects of Text Interventions Leveraging LLMs* (CausalDANN), 2024; arXiv:2410.21474. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21474>. A parallel LLM-counterfactual approach that frames the problem as domain adaptation rather than DML, and reports gains on semi-synthetic benchmarks.
